metadata.document_subject: Nature finance is essential to halt and reverse biodiversity loss – one of the most urgent crises affecting our planet. There is compelling evidence that nature is best conserved when it is managed by Indigenous Peoples and local communities, including local actors such as smallholder farmers, fishers and pastoralists. Local actors must therefore have leadership over how projects are implemented and funds are spent in their territories. However, evidence on how much nature finance is reaching the local level or is locally led is lacking. This report uses a keyword search methodology to explore trends in international nature finance flows and estimate how much is implemented with local actors, and how much is locally led. We also estimate how much of this finance is reaching Indigenous Peoples and is Indigenous led.

chunks.text: LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE 6 Summary Biodiversity loss is one of the most urgent crises affecting our planet. Species extinction rates are higher than ever before in human history, with over a million plant and animal species expected to become extinct over the coming decades if no action is taken (IPBES, 2019). To address this problem, financial flows will need to be redirected and reconfigured to move our economic activities away from activities that harm nature (such as deforestation, agricultural expansion and mining), and towards activities that benefit and restore nature (such as conservation, agroforestry and agroecology). Nature finance is therefore essential to halt and reverse the biodiversity loss crisis. The Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) includes two ambitious targets on nature finance (Targets 18 and 19) that seek to close the US$700 billion biodiversity funding gap — including to raise US$200 billion of new finance per year and redirect US$500 billion of harmful subsidies per year by 2030. However, the existing funding vehicles established to channel this finance, such as the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund (GBFF) and the Cali Fund, have so far not delivered at the scale required. Furthermore, the targets lack attention to how much finance will reach the communities who live closest to nature around the world and who possess the best knowledge and skills to protect it, especially Indigenous Peoples (IPs) and local communities (LCs). Crucially, for nature finance to meet the needs of these communities, be rights-based and be effective at halting and restoring nature, projects must be led by local actors rather than just implemented alongside them but designed externally. The principles for locally led adaptation (LLA) and the principles for inclusive nature action (INA) provide valuable frameworks to guide nature finance funders and policymakers on how to channel locally led finance. While these principles have received wide endorsement in policy spaces, evidence on how much nature finance actually aligns with these principles, and is locally led, is lacking. In this report, we explore trends in international nature finance flows to estimate how much is implemented with local actors and how much is locally led. ‘Locally led’ and ‘locally implemented’ funding are considered here not as the same thing but as distinct concepts; funding can be implemented at the local level without being driven by the priorities of local actors or implemented by them directly. Locally implemented nature action is usually designed by external stakeholders rather than the communities themselves and so can still miss the mark in terms of meeting the needs of local actors and ensuring they have agency to design and implement projects in their own way. On the other hand, nature action that is locally led ensures local actors play a leading role in the design, implementation, decision making and governance of nature projects (see Box 3). While efforts have been made previously to calculate the amount of funding reaching the local level, we did not find any existing studies that aimed to determine how much nature finance is locally led (as opposed to locally implemented, or targeting the local level in some way). This analysis uses a keyword search methodology adapted from a previous study by Treichel et al. in 2025 (see Box 1).

chunks.text: SUMMARY 7 Box 1. Studies that informed this research The study by Treichel et al. (2025) is foundational for this report; it in turn leant on the approaches by Soanes et al. in 2017 and Watkiss et al. in 2023. Treichel et al. analysed flows of climate finance to the local level using the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Assistance Committee’s (OECD DAC) Climate-Related Development Finance (CRDF) data and applied a keyword search methodology to funding tagged with the climate-related Rio markers. The Treichel et al. study found that 29% of the climate finance descriptions and titles include some reference to local implementation and 0.17% of finance mentions locally led climate action. In this report, we adapt the methodology and apply it to the OECD DAC official development assistance (ODA) data marked with the Rio marker for biodiversity over 2011–2024. Our key findings show that, of the ODA reported to the OECD DAC between 2021 and 2024 tagged for biodiversity: • 33.7% of the funding line descriptions or titles include some reference to the local level, with only 0.28% referring to ‘locally led’,1 and • 2.24% include some reference to ‘Indigenous Peoples’ or other related keywords, with only 0.001% referring to ‘Indigenous led’. Figure 1 illustrates how small a proportion of overall nature finance even includes any mention of local implementation or local actors and how extremely tiny the proportion is that is locally or Indigenous led. It also demonstrates how data constraints limit our ability to accurately estimate total funding amounts flowing to local actors, which would fall somewhere in between. Figure 1. chunks.text: LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE 8 The findings are deeply concerning, as they indicate that even where money is spent at the local level, or there are benefits for local actors, over 99% of nature projects are still led by non-local actors. IPs and LCs who steward nature may still lack decision making power and agency over how funding is spent in their territories. While nature finance with some local implementation is increasing, the results reveal that almost 70% of all biodiversity funding included no reference to the local level at all. Furthermore, within the nature finance that refers to local implementation, we found that only 2.89% mention the specific term ‘Indigenous Peoples’ and 6.64% mention any keywords related to ‘Indigenous’. We can conclude, therefore, that most (more than 90%) local-level funding goes to non-Indigenous actors. The term ‘Indigenous led’ was only found six times in around 233,000 funding lines over 2011–2024, indicating that leadership of IPs is still barely recognised in nature finance. This suggests that the vast majority of finance implemented with IPs is still designed and led externally. We also discuss how nature finance is delivered, including the sources of finance, the financial instruments used and the trends in commitment versus disbursement data (how much finance is ‘committed’ by donors through pledges or other agreements, versus how much is actually dispensed). The United States was found to be the second largest funder for projects using ‘locally led’ search terms. Since the vast majority of US funding over 2011–2024 was provided via the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the withdrawal of USAID funding in 2025 means that we can reasonably expect to see funding for locally led nature action plummet from 2025 onwards. Preliminary data on 2025 figures from the OECD DAC suggests that overall, ODA has declined significantly from 2024, with many other funders also reducing their contributions (OECD, 2026). This can be expected to have a damaging impact on nature finance, including finance to the local level and finance that is either Indigenous or locally led. The Global Environment Facility (GEF) — the primary multilateral fund delivering nature finance and host of the flagship financial mechanism of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), the GBFF — was found to provide only 1.65% of total reported nature finance. However, there is a particular methodological challenge related to the way GEF funding is reported to the OECD DAC, which means this is likely an underestimate. It is too early to assess the impact of the GBFF on biodiversity or local-level funding since it only began operating in 2023 and disbursement data is not yet available via the OECD DAC data that we use as our source. On the intersection between nature finance and climate finance, we argue that separating climate and nature finance streams matters for ‘upstream’ accounting discussions to track progress against the different goals of the Rio conventions2 and to hold funders to account for their financial commitments to ensure funds are not double-counted.

On the intersection between nature finance and climate finance, we argue that separating climate and nature finance streams matters for ‘upstream’ accounting discussions to track progress against the different goals of the Rio conventions2 and to hold funders to account for their financial commitments to ensure funds are not double-counted. However, this separation can be actively harmful for its effectiveness ‘downstream’, since it can lead to projects being designed with limited scope, or worse, to the exclusion of the needs of key actors on the ground, in whose name such funding is provided in the first place. Efforts should be made in international policy to break down the siloes between nature and climate and streamline local-level finance for these issues under unified funding channels. The report concludes with several recommendations for nature finance policymakers and funding bodies, as well as recommendations for further research. These include: • More finance for nature needs to reach the local level and more needs to be locally led. Additionally, more finance for nature needs to reach IPs and be led by IPs. • Specific indicators should be introduced to the OECD DAC and other reporting frameworks, such as the GBF monitoring framework and GEF indicators for the GBFF, to accurately measure how much finance reaches local actors and how much is locally led. Within the OECD DAC reporting, a first step would be to expand the existing channel of delivery codes to allow subcategories to clearly distinguish between local funding recipients based in funder countries from those in recipient countries. In addition, funders should engage in substantive dialogue with IPs to assess the extent to which projects are in line with the priorities of IPs and to explore the development of appropriate tracking mechanisms. 2 The Rio conventions refer to the three separate UN conventions established in 1992 at the Rio Earth Summit to address the interconnected challenges of climate change, biodiversity loss and desertification. chunks.text: SUMMARY 9 • International policy debates should focus more attention on bilateral funding sources as they currently dominate the nature finance landscape. There is currently an over-emphasis on the multilateral funds, especially the GEF, in nature finance policy discussions, which diminishes the responsibility of funder countries, especially in terms of the provision of grant/concessional finance for nature. • In response to the withdrawal of large amounts of USAID funding, all funders should increase their focus on delivering more locally led finance for nature. This is now needed more than ever and there is potential for small changes to have a significant impact. • The GEF, as the key multilateral funder channelling funding to deliver the GBF targets, should focus on meeting the target of getting 20% of funds to IPs and LCs within the GBFF and apply this across its wider funding portfolio. • The use of debt instruments for nature finance should be minimised. Where they are used, they should be designed in ways that ensure the finance reaches the local level and can be locally led. They must respect the rights and values of IPs and LCs, with full adherence to self-determination and free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) processes. • Funder countries should collectively agree upon consistent reporting approaches to ensure transparent and consistent tracking of their funding commitments. Efforts should be made to streamline this process to avoid double counting and to reduce ‘over-tagging’ of projects with the Rio markers. • Policy negotiations on finance within the CBD and United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) should aim to channel nature and climate finance through joint funding streams to ensure finance addresses both issues holistically. We urge parties to the CBD negotiations on resource mobilisation, financial mechanism and the monitoring framework to consider these recommendations and address them at the 2026 UN Biodiversity Conference (CBD COP17) and beyond.

chunks.text: LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE 10 1 Introduction Biodiversity loss is one of the most urgent crises affecting our planet. Species extinction rates are higher than ever before in human history, with over a million plant and animal species expected to become extinct over the coming decades if no action is taken (IPBES, 2019). Many of the Earth’s valuable ecosystems are at risk of collapse, with severe consequences for the natural resources we depend on to sustain human life. Without nature, the food, water and air we rely on will disappear. However, international funding to conserve these natural resources falls far short of what is needed and the extent to which the funding provided reaches local communities remains unverified. The causes of biodiversity loss are complex and varied, ranging from overconsumption and extraction of natural resources, changes in land and sea use for agriculture and urbanisation, climate change, pollution, and invasive species (UNEP, 2023a). The solutions to these issues are similarly complex and require a multisectoral response. However, one thing that is clear is that financial flows will need to be redirected and reconfigured to move our economic activities away from activities that harm nature (such as deforestation, agricultural expansion and mining) and towards activities that benefit and restore nature (such as conservation, agroforestry and agroecology). Nature finance is essential to halt and reverse the biodiversity loss crisis. In this report, we define ‘nature finance’ as finance that is beneficial for nature and biodiversity: the flow of funds from all sources to conserve biodiversity, ecosystems and species and support positive outcomes for people.3 Nature finance is closely related to climate finance (which refers to finance for climate mitigation, adaptation and loss and damage), with many of the same funders and recipients used for international nature finance and international climate finance, often also using similar types of governance mechanisms to manage and track their flows. However, they can also be administered, implemented and sometimes generated differently because they relate to two different Rio conventions: CBD and UNFCCC. While most nature finance also has positive benefits for climate, the opposite is not always true. Nonetheless, we acknowledge that the distinction between ‘nature finance’ and ‘climate finance’ outside of international policy discussions can seem artificial — and often meaningless — for local communities experiencing the direct impacts of these issues. These contributions fall far short of the GBF target to raise US$200 billion per year for nature. While raising new finance for nature is important, it is only half of the story. GBF commitments are focused on national levels, but biodiversity loss impacts are felt locally, especially by IPs and LCs. These are the people who steward nature globally and possess the best knowledge and skills to protect it. There is compelling evidence that nature is best conserved when it is managed by IPs and LCs, including local actors such as smallholder farmers and fishers and pastoralists (IPBES, 2019; Fa et al., 2020; Dawson et al., 2021; Dawson et al., 2024). Even more important than raising new finance, therefore, is to ensure that the finance we already have is reaching these groups; and any new finance raised will only be effective if it is channelled in the same way. What is missing from the GBF targets is the aim to channel finance directly to IPs and LCs. The GBFF, Cali Fund and TFFF all include a target to direct 20% of their funding to IPs and LCs, but it is unclear how this is being implemented or monitored. Previous tracking studies have been unable to determine how much funding from the GEF reaches IPs and LCs (Sorsby et al., 2025). Furthermore, the targets do not specify that the funding must reach Indigenous or local organisations directly, meaning in many cases funding can pass to an international agency or nongovernmental organisation (NGO) and still fulfil the criteria provided that the project intends to deliver benefits for IPs and LCs. Clearer and more explicit targets to ensure that funding is put directly into the hands of Indigenous and local organisations and for them to have full control over allocation of resources and decision making, are still lacking. 1.2 Locally led nature action Securing direct access to funding has been a key priority for IPs and LCs within global policy for many decades, both for nature and climate finance. Earlier studies have defined ‘local’ institutions as both formal and informal organisations that operate at sub-national level (Soanes et al., 2021; Treichel et al., 2025; Patel, 2024). Local actors can therefore include: • Public entities: subnational authorities and governments that are responsible for meeting local needs • Private entities: formal and informal enterprises • Civil society: community-based organisations, IPs organisations, local groups and social movements, and • Households and individuals: those that share administrative units, a sense of community, locality or shocks and stresses. Our definition of ‘local’ is similar to the OECD’s working definition (OECD, 2024d), which includes actors who are based in and centred on local issues, subject to local laws and operating within the local context. While both our definition and the OECD’s definition exclude international NGOs and their country offices, multilateral organisations and international private-sector organisations, a key distinction is that, unlike the OECD, our definition excludes national governments. We consider ‘local’ to imply communities or connected groups of people who are likely to have shared experiences of climate and nature impacts (Rahman et al., 2023). In particular, we recognise IPs as important rights holders for locally led action on nature and aim to distinguish activities led, directed and implemented by IPs from those at the general community level. In sum, we use the following definitions in this report to distinguish between the different types of ‘local level’ nature finance: • Nature action implemented with local actors: biodiversity actions that involve community members as beneficiaries or that are implemented at the local level. This includes funding that targets a specific community, or is spent within that community, but is not necessarily driven by the priorities of local actors or implemented by them directly. Funding for locally led nature action would not only reach local actors directly, they would also play a leading role in the design, implementation, decision making and governance of nature projects. • Nature action implemented with IPs: biodiversity actions that involve IPs as beneficiaries or are implemented with IPs. This includes funding that targets IPs, or is spent within their territories, but is not necessarily driven by their priorities or implemented by them directly. chunks.text: LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE 14 These existing studies offer a helpful foundation for our analysis. While efforts have been made previously to calculate the amount of funding reaching the local level, no existing study was found that aimed to determine how much nature finance is locally led (as opposed to locally implemented, or targeting the local level in some way). Our research is also focused on ODA — that is, on ‘development aid’ — rather than ODF. ODF goes beyond ODA and also includes non- concessional development resources and other official flows (OOF) that do not meet the criteria to be considered development aid, such as export credits or loans provided at market rates. The present study aims to complement the existing research in this area by analysing the full set of development aid data from the OECD DAC tagged with the Rio marker for biodiversity to estimate (1) how much nature-focused ODA is reaching the local level and (2) how much nature-focused ODA is locally led. We also aim to estimate how much nature‑focused ODA is going to IPs specifically, as important rights holders for local action on nature, and how much nature-focused ODA is Indigenous led. The study also offers some insights into nature finance reaching urban areas and the sources and types of nature finance, and offers reflections on the relationship between locally led nature finance and locally led climate finance. This report builds directly on the methodology used by Treichel et al. in 2025. That study analysed the OECD DAC’s CRDF data and found that 29% of climate finance includes some reference to local implementation and 0.17% of funding mentions locally led climate action. The actual amount of funding reaching the local level is unknowable from the data available. In this report, we adapt the methodology and apply it to the OECD DAC ODA data marked with the Rio marker for biodiversity. We use a keyword search methodology adapted from similar prior studies (Treichel et al., 2025; OECD, 2024a; Sorsby et al., 2025). Crucially, we look only at ODA finance and not at other investments that are non-ODA. As a result, our findings are limited to OECD DAC member countries. For consistency with previous studies, we look at nature finance from 2011–2024 to observe trends over time. We also offer early insights into how locally led nature finance differs from locally led climate finance, as per the results found by Treichel et al. in 2025, noting the two studies are not directly comparable for reasons outlined in Section 3.3.2. The remainder of this report is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines our methodology and limitations, Section 3 presents our results and a discussion of the findings and Section 4 presents recommendations for nature finance policymakers and funding bodies.

Detailed methodology), which in turn leant on the approaches by Soanes et al. in 2017 and Watkiss et al. in 2023: First, we sourced and refined the best available dataset. This means that all countries remaining after the ‘category’ filter was applied (to exclude non-ODA) are included. Note that the EU is an OECD DAC member and treated in the CRS and in this report as bilateral. The CRS dataset includes both commitment and disbursement data. In this report, we examine disbursement data rather than commitment data — that is, we look at how much money OECD DAC members actually gave to countries in a given year, rather than how much they committed to countries in that year. Disbursement data seems a more accurate set of figures to use to answer the question of how much funding is reaching the local level, but commitment data is more commonly used in reporting (see, for example, OECD, 2020; OECD, 2024a) and so our figures may not be comparable to other reports. Disbursement data may be less smooth year-on-year, as it will reflect funding transmission issues within individual years that are masked by commitment data, but it is more accurate in that it only reflects funding that is actually disbursed; commitments that are made but not realised are not included. If commitments were always realised, disbursement data would follow very similar patterns to commitment data, with slight lags to reflect the time difference between commitments and implementation. As shown in our results section, this is often not the case and so we use disbursement data as our default.

chunks.text: METHODOLOGY 17 2.2 Limitations There are five key limitations of using the OECD DAC data for our research: • First, one consequence of only looking at ODA as reported via the OECD DAC is that we exclude other forms of international finance not categorised as development assistance. This means we do not include either private- sector or philanthropic funding, or other international finance covered by ODF, such as via non-concessional loans or export credits. This means our findings may differ from other reports that include ODF. This source of data is also not exhaustive and so will not include ‘non-tagged’ nature finance; it also cannot include other flows of nature finance not captured through OECD DAC reporting. The purpose of this report is to look at how much of the nature-focused development finance provided over the 2011–2024 period targets the local level or is locally or Indigenous led. • Second, there are well-known limitations to the OECD DAC datasets, particularly around potential over-tagging of the Rio markers by funders — that is, funding lines being marked as relevant to the Rio treaties when, in fact, they are not (Hicks et al., 2008; Roberts and Weikmans, 2017; Wood and Leng, 2025). This issue has been especially well documented for climate; we assume the same tendency applies for biodiversity. This research did not attempt to validate the relevance of the funding marked with the Rio marker for biodiversity. • Third, this over-tagging leads to questions about the overall accuracy of the OECD DAC data (Doshi and Garschagen, 2020; Weikmans et al., 2017). We also did not verify the funding values in the OECD DAC data — our focus is on the proportion of funding targeting the local level and for locally led nature action. For this purpose, the OECD DAC data provides a relatively robust dataset; but to verify estimates of the total quantity of funding provided, this data would need to be compared to other datasets, for example, from end recipients. This is beyond the scope of this work; throughout this report we use proportions rather than total funding amounts. • Fourth, as outlined in the methodology section above, there is no biodiversity dataset equivalent to the CRDF dataset that was used in Treichel et al. While the acceptance of ideas may well be demonstrated by increased reference to them, it is important that in this report, when we call for increases in funding for particular keywords — especially for locally led and Indigenous-led nature action — we are seeking an increase in the effective implementation of those concepts, rather than only for increases in funding, and certainly not only for an increase in the use of terminology.

chunks.text: LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE 18 • Selecting keywords to indicate ‘local’ is ambiguous and subjective and open to multiple interpretations of how ‘local’ is defined. As above, we significantly expanded and refined the keyword list from previous attempts — see Appendix 1 for a full list. For example, we expanded the search terms beyond ‘locally led’ and ‘community led’ used by Treichel et al. to also include ‘Indigenous led’ in this research, given the unique importance of IPs and LCs as nature stewards around the world. We also significantly expanded the French and Spanish translations of keywords to capture more of the reported funding. While this process of expanding and refining the keyword set has allowed us to improve our approach and increase the accuracy of our searching (as both missed data and the number of false positives should be significantly decreased), expanding the set of keywords does also open up further questions about how we define ‘local’. For example, terms like ‘gatherer’, ‘hunter’, ‘mother earth’, ‘peasant’ and ‘tenure’ would not normally be considered synonyms for ‘local’ in regular conversation. However, project descriptions that include these terms are likely to be implemented at the local level. What this demonstrates is the complicated nature of what we mean by ‘local’ and the difficulties in accurately drawing a boundary around this definition. We have done multiple rounds of testing and review of the words selected, and of examining their use in project descriptions to eliminate words that yield too many false positives or are otherwise inappropriate, in line with our definition articulated in Box 4, but the philosophical question of what counts as local remains (see Jarillo and Barnett, 2021; Panelli and Welch, 2005). • A key limitation of this research overall is that we have only performed quantitative analysis on the OECD DAC ODA data, but have not gathered inputs from funding recipients. Qualitative data from funding recipients would be needed to corroborate the degree to which funded activities genuinely involve local actors or are locally led. While this step is beyond the scope of the present study, we acknowledge that the findings can only represent a partial picture of where funding really ends up and how. Our methodology also cannot tell us anything about the lived experience of implementing nature finance at the local level, to what extent local actors are able to lead projects or to what extent projects are in line with, and designed to respond to, the self-determined needs and priorities of IPs and LCs. chunks.text: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 21 3.1.2 Nature finance to the local level The proportion of nature finance targeting the local level (but not necessarily locally led) has been variable over time (see Figure 3). While the overall trend has been gently upward, there are large year-on-year differences and some backsliding over this timeframe. The overall upward trend in local-level funding allocation aligns closely with the welcome overall trend for increases in nature finance. While Figure 3 also shows clear yearly variations between both the commitment and disbursement data, there is no clear trend between commitments in one year and disbursements in the year or two that follow (as might be expected). However, the total proportion of nature finance with some local implementation is very close, with 33.7% of the disbursement funding and 32.2% for the commitment funding. This is consistent with other studies that found that approximately 30% of GEF-7 biodiversity finance was targeted towards IPs and LCs (Sorsby et al., 2025). However, it differs from others, such as the OECD study that found that only 8% of OECD DAC members’ biodiversity-related ODF was targeted towards IPs and LCs (OECD, forthcoming). This is likely because our study only looks at ODA, whereas the OECD study looked at ODF, which includes other types of finance, including non-concessional and private-sector finance. The overall upward trend is also consistent with the Path to Scale funding dashboard (Path to Scale, no date), which shows an approximate increase of US$500 million in total funding for IP, LC and Afro-descendant Peoples’ tenure rights between 2011 and 2024. Our finding is also similar to that of Treichel et al. (2025), which found that approximately 29% of total reported climate finance included some reference to local implementation. Despite these positive indications, the results reveal that over 70% of all funding for biodiversity is not targeted towards the local level at all. Given the critical importance of actions by local actors such as IPs and LCs in protecting and restoring biodiversity, this finding is concerning. Furthermore, there is no way to determine whether the funding corresponding to the projects that referred to local implementation actually reached local actors or organisations directly, or whether it was just directed at the local level by a national or international intermediary organisation and included an indirect benefit for local actors. Note again that each funding line may contain more than one keyword, so these percentages cannot be added together. Comparison of highest frequency word use with highest funding amounts shows that although the top four keywords remain consistent regardless of which metric is used, for other words, there is considerable variation. For example, ‘provinc*’ is the keyword with the fifth highest amount of nature finance, but is only the eleventh most frequently used keyword overall. ‘City’ is the eighth highest in terms of the amount of nature finance, but is not in the top ten for frequency of use — it drops to sixteenth for both total number of matches and number of individual funding lines in which the word appears (a keyword may be used multiple times in any individual funding line). This suggests that for both of these keywords — ‘city’ and ‘provinc*’ — they are included in funding lines with higher value than the average. On the other hand, ‘Indigen*’ ranks more highly for keyword frequency (fifth in terms of both total matches and the total number of individual funding lines that it appears in) than it does for total amount of funding including this keyword (where it is seventh), suggesting this keyword is included in projects worth lower funding amounts. In general, the commitment figures are higher than the disbursement figures, but follow the same broad trends in terms of the proportion targeting local and Indigenous nature actors or for locally or Indigenous-led nature action. Overall, of the finance reported by OECD DAC members between 2011 and 2024 tagged for biodiversity, we found that 32.2% of funding committed is targeting the local level compared to 33.7% for disbursed funding, and 0.28% of funding committed is locally led compared to 0.31% for disbursed funding. Bilaterals used debt in 18.4% of nature ODA targeting the local level and in 22.2% of all nature ODA. In both cases, debt use was lower for funding that involved any ‘local’ keywords. Particular funders demonstrate a much higher preference for debt instruments for nature finance than others. For example, 97.9% of all debt provided by bilaterals for nature finance was provided by just four countries: Canada, France, Germany and Japan. chunks.text: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 29 3.3.4 Using OECD DAC categories While the OECD DAC provides the most extensive dataset for tracking flows of development aid finance, there are some shortcomings specific to tracking local flows (see Section 2.2 on limitations). Chief among these is the lack of an inbuilt indicator that distinguishes local from non-local flows.9 The OECD DAC data does include a category titled ‘channel of delivery’. This describes the initial recipient of funding — there may be other recipients further along the delivery chain, but this category reflects the first recipient to receive the reported funding. Unfortunately, this category doesn’t easily allow for tracking of local-level recipients. This is partly because local recipients may well not be the initial recipients of funding but are further along the funding chain, and also because the categories are not well suited to reflecting our definitions of ‘local’ (outlined in Box 4). For example, some categories (such as the one for universities and think tanks) do not distinguish between actors based in recipient countries and those in the funder countries. So this data is particularly limited in what it can reveal. The following categories would include local actors (though some would obviously also include local actors within funder countries, who we would exclude from our accounting): • 12002: local governments in recipient countries • 23000: developing country-based NGO • 30000, 31000 and 32000: public–private partnerships and networks • 51000: university, college, research institute or think-tank • 62000: private sector in recipient country Funding channelled to this set of recipients — in other words, delivered directly to subnational actor types within both funder and recipient countries — accounted for only 6.6% of all reported nature finance. That does not align with our keyword search findings, which explore local actors based in recipient countries, for which this figure is 33.7%. Further, there was limited overlap between the funding lines found through these two approaches, with just under half of the funding lines using the above channel of delivery codes using any of our local keywords. This suggests that — despite their potential — the channel of delivery categories are not currently a useful mechanism for estimating flows to local actors. Treichel et al. (2025) similarly explored the channel of delivery as a means to explore first-order funding recipients and made recommendations for improving this reporting element to allow users to distinguish between funding recipients that are based in funder countries from funding recipients based in recipient countries, and thereby allow clearer analysis of funding flows. metadata.document_subject: Nature finance is essential to halt and reverse biodiversity loss – one of the most urgent crises affecting our planet. There is compelling evidence that nature is best conserved when it is managed by Indigenous Peoples and local communities, including local actors such as smallholder farmers, fishers and pastoralists. Local actors must therefore have leadership over how projects are implemented and funds are spent in their territories. However, evidence on how much nature finance is reaching the local level or is locally led is lacking. This report uses a keyword search methodology to explore trends in international nature finance flows and estimate how much is implemented with local actors, and how much is locally led. We also estimate how much of this finance is reaching Indigenous Peoples and is Indigenous led.

chunks.text: LOCALLY LED FINANCE FOR NATURE 30 4 Conclusions and recommendations Our analysis reveals that only a tiny proportion of total reported nature finance is Indigenous or locally led. A lack of dedicated mechanisms to track funding to the local level limits the ability to accurately estimate total funding amounts for local actors; however, the keyword search approach reveals that proportions for local and Indigenous actors remain shockingly low. More efforts are needed to improve both the quantity and quality of nature finance for IPs and LCs. Overall, the results of the study show that locally led finance for nature is still lagging far behind where it needs to be to meet global policy commitments and deliver on the LLA and INA principles, which are gaining increasing traction from local and international stakeholders in nature and climate finance policy negotiations. Not only does the quantity of nature finance going to IPs and LCs need to increase, but more attention also needs to be paid to ensuring that IPs and LCs lead throughout the design, implementation, decision making and governance of projects. Furthermore, formal mechanisms to consistently track funding reaching the local level are lacking. There are currently no appropriate indicators for local-level engagement or processes to maintain transparency over funding flows within the key reporting frameworks for donors, such as the OECD DAC. Keyword search methodology, despite its many limitations, is therefore the best tool currently available for tracking these trends. Similarly, the OECD dataset and the Rio marker system remain the best available resources to monitor overall nature finance flows, despite their critiques. There is a clear need for more studies backed by on-the-ground data from funding recipients to complement the tracking that is done on data provided by the funders. Based on these findings, we present the following recommendations for nature finance policymakers and funding bodies, as well as recommendations for further research. We urge parties to the CBD negotiations on resource mobilisation, financial mechanism and the monitoring framework to consider these recommendations and address them at CBD COP17 and beyond. Recommendations on the quantity of nature finance: • More finance for nature needs to reach the local level, and more needs to be locally led. Additionally, more finance for nature needs to reach IPs and be led by IPs. This is critically important given the unique role of IPs in conserving and restoring nature. • Specific indicators should be introduced to the OECD DAC and other reporting frameworks, such as the GBF monitoring framework and GEF indicators applied to the GBFF, to accurately measure how much finance reaches local actors and how much is locally led. chunks.text: CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 31 • More finance for nature should be directed towards urban areas to fund nature-based solution projects and conserve natural biodiversity in cities. Further research is needed to determine why finance for nature in cities is not reaching the most vulnerable communities and slum dwellers. Recommendations on how nature finance is delivered: • Increases in commitments should theoretically result in increased disbursements, yet our data shows this is often not the case. As such, studies to estimate funding reaching end users should focus on disbursement data rather than commitment data. • Moreover, each of the above recommendations highlights the importance of increasing the amount of finance reaching local actors — this should not mean merely increasing the use of local or locally led keywords in descriptions of finance, but for increases to translate to actual differences on the ground. metadata.document_title: Locally led finance for nature: estimating finance flows to local actors for conserving and restoring nature
metadata.document_subject: Nature finance is essential to halt and reverse biodiversity loss – one of the most urgent crises affecting our planet. There is compelling evidence that nature is best conserved when it is managed by Indigenous Peoples and local communities, including local actors such as smallholder farmers, fishers and pastoralists. Local actors must therefore have leadership over how projects are implemented and funds are spent in their territories. However, evidence on how much nature finance is reaching the local level or is locally led is lacking. This report uses a keyword search methodology to explore trends in international nature finance flows and estimate how much is implemented with local actors, and how much is locally led. We also estimate how much of this finance is reaching Indigenous Peoples and is Indigenous led.

chunks.text: Diabetes Health Prediction and Analysis Using Machine Learning Bharath Krishna Department of Computer Science Engineering Email: your@email.com Abstract—Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disorder that affects millions of individuals worldwide and requires early detection to prevent severe health complications. This study presents a comprehensive Diabetes Health Prediction and Analysis system that leverages machine learning techniques to predict the likeli- hood of diabetes in patients. The proposed framework integrates data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis (EDA), feature engineering, and model development into a unified pipeline. Multiple classification algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost, are trained and evaluated using standard performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. Experimental results demonstrate that ensemble-based models outperform traditional methods, with XGBoost achieving the highest accuracy of 91.76% and ROC-AUC of 98.41%. The system also includes a web-based application for real-time predic- tion, enhancing usability for practical healthcare scenarios. This work highlights the effectiveness of machine learning in medical diagnosis and provides a scalable solution for early diabetes detection and analysis. Keywords—Diabetes Prediction, Machine Learning, Health- care Analytics, Artificial Intelligence, Feature Engineering, XG- Boost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Data Preprocessing, Predictive Modeling, Clinical Decision Support System, Health Monitoring, Data Mining, Medical Diagnosis, Chatbot Integra- tion. I. INTRODUCTION Diabetes mellitus is one of the most prevalent non- communicable diseases globally, characterized by high blood glucose levels resulting from defects in insulin production or function. Early diagnosis plays a crucial role in managing the disease and reducing long-term complications such as cardiovascular diseases, kidney failure, and neuropathy. With the rapid growth of healthcare data, machine learning techniques have emerged as powerful tools for disease pre- diction and decision support. These techniques can identify hidden patterns in medical datasets, enabling accurate and effi- cient diagnosis. In this context, predictive modeling has gained significant importance in assisting healthcare professionals. This project presents a structured and end-to-end pipeline for diabetes prediction using machine learning. The workflow begins with data preprocessing to handle missing values and inconsistencies, followed by exploratory data analysis to understand feature distributions and correlations. Feature engineering techniques are then applied to enhance model performance. Multiple models, including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost, are trained and evaluated to identify the best-performing approach. Additionally, the system integrates a user-friendly web ap- plication that allows real-time predictions based on user input. The combination of analytical insights and predictive modeling makes this system a valuable tool for healthcare analysis and decision-making. II. METHODOLOGY The proposed system follows a multi-stage data-driven pipeline for real-time diabetes prediction and analysis. A. Data Acquisition The system collects patient health data either from a struc- tured dataset or through user input via a web interface. The input includes key medical parameters such as BMI, glucose level, blood pressure, and lifestyle-related attributes. B. Data Preprocessing The acquired data undergoes preprocessing to ensure quality and consistency. Missing values are handled using mean imputation, categorical variables are encoded into numerical format, and all numerical features are normalized using z-score standardization to maintain uniform scale. C. Feature Engineering To enhance predictive performance, new features are gen- erated. Interaction features such as Age × BMI are created to capture relationships between variables. Additionally, poly- nomial feature expansion (degree = 2) is applied to model non- linear patterns in the data. D. Model Training (Machine Learning) Multiple supervised learning algorithms are trained using the processed dataset: • Logistic Regression for baseline performance • Random Forest for ensemble-based learning • XGBoost for optimized gradient boosting These models learn patterns from the training data to accurately classify diabetes risk.
